Sorry kiddo but I actually know a thing or two about propagation of light from coherent sources. Even if all the transmitters were broadcasting exactly the same thing you will still get interference due to the baseline between the two transmitters. This presumes that you have somehow overcome the problem of perfectly synchronising several sources at several GHz. The simplest equipment that could do that costs more than a house.

This is not like a fiber where the medium is carefully controlled. Not even close.

For this to work you must insure that the receiver sees one and only one transmitter at a time. Not even the slightest reflection from another transmitter.

The light doesn't need to be coherent, it is being pulsed (like PWM), so the only thing that would matter is the length of the pulse which could vary (I have no idea how what they have made works at the moment) depending on how far the APs are apart.

for example, if they wanted pulses that could deal with path length differences that were ~1m then they would be looking at around 300MHz (c/1M) ~ 300Mbps (with no error correction or any other overhead), but that is per frequency. This could be done on multiple wavelengths, so a 4LED transmitter could probably do the 1Gbps.

The PWM modulation and the fundamental wavelength of the light you are transmitting are two separate parameters. Both introduce their separate interferences. This complicates things a great deal, especially when both are close to each other. So we end up talking of wave packets and wave envelopes instead of distinct pulses. So we have to deal with fun things like group velocity and phase velocity.

So the light source must be coherent and monochromatic, otherwise you won't be able to tell when a pulse has done arriving. It introduces uncertainty (a sort of smear) of several picoseconds which will kill your data rate. It is like a blur in an image when you are trying to count individual blades of grass.

This is why data transmission with broad spectrum light sources doesn't work nearly as well. In order to be able to count the individual pulses you have to slow way down.

They'd trivially be able to tell exactly who this affected. In other words, if you didn't get an email - don't worry about it.

Amazon, like most remotely competent sites, doesn't store your password and doesn't know your password. They could give you their entire database of passwords and you couldn't do anything with it. The way this works is that when you send your password to Amazon they don't actually store your password but instead an 'encrypted' (not the most precise term, but this is an ELI5 and it uses the same mathematical concepts as encryption - which is under fire) version of your password. So "password123" becomes "FJ#$Ngn4u6!@." So when you login they encrypt your password and then compare it to what's stored to see if they match.

The great thing about this is that it makes server side password hacks impossible. Amazon could email you their password database and there's practically nothing you could do with it. Even if you try to get clever and say "Well I know how they encrypt passwords and I know lots of people use "password123" as their password, let me encrypt "password123" and see if anybody in this database has this encrypted value as their password. This is overcome by 'salting'. What this is that instead of simply encrypting password123 they encrypt password123 and a random string of characters that's unique to your account. This string would also be in the database but it means for a hacker to hack any account they'd have to brute force it. Eg - even if 2 people are both using "password123" for one person the value that's stored will be the encrypted version of "password123FHJFnfnbtu4" and the other person will have the encrypted version of "password123Gnnfbu6k". The hacker would be able to see, in plain text, FHJFnfnbtu4 and Gnnfbu6k but it stops him from hacking the entire database by brute force, which would start turning up hits pretty rapidly.
